newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS--Brazil green soybean sales take off.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS--Brazil green soybean sales take off.

text.p: With an estimated 80 to 90 percent of Brazil's 1995/96 soybean crop sold, the trade has now begun in earnest to make advance sales of its 1996/97 crop, so-called green soybeans, traders and brokers said.
"We reckon 20 percent of the coming harvest has already been sold," said one leading Parana state based broker. "Most cooperatives and traders are now making green soybean sales."
A leading Rio Grande do Sul broker said he was recommending clients to sell some of the crop, either for the domestic or export market, because the price is so good.
"The price is really fantastic," he said. "If we'd have had these prices three to four years ago people would have gone crazy with advance crop sales."
"The current problem is lack of available funds in the market, especially among export customers," he said.

Green soybean sales, traditionally popular in Brazil, but which lack any guarantee, fell out of favor over the last two years due to farmers' debt problems, which led to cases of non-delivery of the soybeans to contracted customers.

For the coming soybean season, however, most farmers are in a far improved situation due to the government's drawing up of debt securitisation programmes with producers, and this year's long run of favorable domestic and international prices.
The national soybean price, a composite average, was quoted at $17.06 a 60-kilo bag on September 19, some $3 above the price of just one month previously.
Prices at Rio Grande port for sale delivered to crushers reached 19.20 reais ($19) this week, dipping slightly at the week's end to 18.80 reais ($18.61), said broker Brasoja.

At Paranagua port Alianca Corretora reported sales of soybean delivered to crushers at 18.50 reais ($18.31) per 60-kilo bag on September 19, while green soybeans were fetching 16.50 reais ($16.34) for April 1997 delivery.

Traders and brokers estimated Brazil's 1996/97 soybean crop may be up to 15 percent bigger than this year's, reaching some 27 million tonnes, giving plenty of scope for producers wishing to sell green soybeans.
Planting is expected to begin during October.

The numbers of soybean futures contracts traded on Sao Paulo's futures exchange Bolsa de Mercadorias e de Futuros (BM&F) has meanwhile grown relatively slowly since the contract's launch in late 1995.
In the month of August 1996, 2,042 soybean futures contracts were traded on the BM&F, worth 13.4 million reais ($13.27 million), an exchange spokesman said.
Trade sources said they feel the Brazilian soybean market is not sufficiently large to support a full-level futures market.

"The trade is worried price distortions could arise between the futures market and the cash market, especially as liquidation in the futures contract is via a cash index rather than product," one broker said.
"That's why the trade prefers green soybean sales, even despite the lack of guarantees," he said.
For what remains of Brazil's 1995/96 crop, traders and brokers described the Brazilian market as continuing nervously quiet in view of the soycomplex price fluctuations in Chicago.
Only isolated sales are now taking place from the current year's crop, they said.

This follows a flurry of activity earlier in the week immediately following the government's elimination of the state-level ICMS tax on exports and interstate sales of soycomplex products, they said. -- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
